newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Bundesbank batters dollar, holds rates.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bundesbank batters dollar, holds rates.

text.p: The Bundesbank on Thursday sent a strong signal to markets that the dollar had risen far enough and moved to calm a fierce debate over the exact meaning of entry criteria for Europe's monetary union.
Meeting in the picturesque Bavarian town of Aschau, the central bank left its credit policies unchanged, as expected.

Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said the German central bank was "closely watching" developments on foreign exchange markets and was determined that the mark would remain strong in the run-up to the euro launch in 1999.

"We are now in a phase in which the correction has clearly come to an end," Tietmeyer said of the dollar which had at its height clocked up gains of more than 14 percent against the mark so far this year.
"We will naturally watch the developments in markets. You can be sure that it is important for us that the mark remains a strong currency and enters the euro as a strong currency."
His comments took almost a pfennig off the dollar, which fell from 1.7620 marks before the news conference to some 1.7540 immediately after. It eased to 1.7515 by 1510 GMT.
Bundesbank council member Franz-Christoph Zeitler reinforced Tietmeyer's commitment to a strong mark when he spoke with reporters after the meeting.

Asked about the dollar's appreciation against the mark this year, Zeitler said the Group of Seven industrial nations meeting at the end of April had determined that the state of correction in the exchange rates had "more or less" come to an end.
"On the other hand, what we do not want is a push in the other direction," he said.

Tietmeyer also said the bank was watching developments on the German share market, which has experienced a boom that added 32 percent to the blue chip DAX index in the first half of 1997, partly fuelled by the dollar gains.

"I don't want to follow in the steps of (Alan) Greenspan," said Tietmeyer, referring to the U.S. Federal Reserve chairman whose warnings of "irrational exuberance" on markets last December sparked a temporary rout on global stock markets.
The central bank left its interest rates unchanged at the meeting in line with economists' expectations. The discount rate remains at 2.50 percent and the Lombard at 4.50 percent.
The Bundesbank made no comment on the Bank of England's decision to raise U.K. interest rates 1/4 point to 6.75 percent which took place shortly after the Bundesbank news conference.
But Tietmeyer noted that the strong exchange rate of the British pound was a reflection of the domestic situation there.

Turning to the thorny issue of which countries will qualify for entry to European Monetary Union in 1999, Tietmeyer said the issue was being clouded by calls for exact numerical adherence to the Maastricht criteria.

He told a news conference that insistence on nations getting their budget deficit down to exactly three percent of their gross domestic product -- a key requirement for EMU -- was obscuring the more important task of achieving sustainable convergence and lasting fiscal discipline.

"It is not appropriate only to look at the zero discussion," Tietmeyer said, referring to calls that the three percent limit must be interpreted as 3.0 percent and not 3.1, 3.2 or higher. "It is more important to look at sustainability which is a criterion of the (Maastricht) Treaty."
Tietmeyer's remarks were an apparent shot across the bows of Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber, who has insisted nations must not be allowed scope to overshoot the three percent level.

Stoiber, who has spearheaded a campaign calling for the strictest possible interpretation of the EMU convergence criteria, was quoted this week as saying it would be better to delay the launch of the single currency, scheduled for 1999, than to risk having a soft euro.

Government sources said on Thursday Germany would meet the 3.0 percent deficit target even though the federal deficit was set to balloon to 71.2 billion marks ($40 billion), up from an earlier forecast of 53.3 billion.

The Bundesbank and finance ministry earlier combined to knock down a report that the Bonn government planned a further change in the Bundesbank's laws which would reduce the size of its policy-making council and give top officials a pay cut.
